subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography - Coasts
subtitle: Reading passages for KS3 coastal geography revision.
description: Five source-grounded reading passages with comprehension questions on waves, landforms, hazards, management and coastal fieldwork.

data.sourcePassage: Waves are mainly caused by wind blowing across the sea. The longer and stronger the wind is, and the further it travels over open water, the more powerful the wave can become. This distance is called the fetch. When a wave reaches shallow water, the bottom of the wave slows as it touches the seabed, while the top keeps moving faster. The wave becomes steeper and breaks. Swash moves water and sediment up the beach, and backwash moves water back down towards the sea. Constructive waves have strong swash and weak backwash, so they usually build beaches. Destructive waves have weak swash and strong backwash, so they usually remove beach material, especially during storms.

questions.modelAnswer: Most sea waves are caused by wind blowing across the sea.

questions.question: Why does a wave break as it reaches shallow water?
questions.modelAnswer: The bottom of the wave slows down because it touches the seabed, while the top keeps moving faster, making the wave steeper until it breaks.

questions.question: Which wave type usually builds beaches?
questions.modelAnswer: Constructive waves usually build beaches because their swash is stronger than their backwash.

questions.question: Explain why winter storms may make a beach narrower.
questions.modelAnswer: Winter storms often bring destructive waves with strong backwash, which can drag sediment down the beach and remove beach material.

data.sourcePassage: Coastal erosion, transportation and deposition work together. Waves can erode cliffs, move the broken material along the shore, and deposit it where energy is lower. Hydraulic action happens when waves force air into cracks, increasing pressure until the rock weakens. Abrasion happens when rocks and sand scrape against cliffs. Attrition makes stones smaller, smoother and rounder as they collide. Transportation can happen by traction, saltation, suspension and solution. Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast when swash travels up the beach at an angle and backwash flows straight back down under gravity. Deposition happens when water loses energy, often in sheltered bays, behind spits or where constructive waves dominate.

questions.question: Name the three main coastal process groups in the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: The three main process groups are erosion, transportation and deposition.

questions.question: Which process involves rocks and sand scraping against cliffs?
questions.modelAnswer: Abrasion involves rocks and sand scraping against cliffs.

questions.question: How does longshore drift move sediment along a beach?
questions.modelAnswer: Swash carries sediment up the beach at an angle and backwash flows straight down under gravity, creating a zigzag movement along the coast.

questions.question: Why are sheltered bays likely places for deposition?
questions.modelAnswer: Sheltered bays often have lower wave energy, so water can no longer carry as much sediment and drops it.

questions.question: Explain how the same piece of sediment might be affected by more than one coastal process.
questions.modelAnswer: It could be broken from a cliff by erosion, moved along the coast by transportation, and later dropped by deposition when wave energy falls.

data.sourcePassage: Many coastal landforms can be explained as sequences. A wave-cut platform forms when waves erode the base of a cliff, creating a notch. As the notch deepens, the cliff above becomes unsupported and collapses. Waves remove the fallen material and the cliff retreats, leaving a flat rocky platform. Headlands and bays form through differential erosion, where softer rock erodes faster than harder rock. On a headland, waves may attack cracks and form caves. If erosion continues, a cave can become an arch. When the arch roof collapses, a stack remains, and further erosion can reduce the stack to a stump. Old Harry Rocks in Dorset are a useful UK example of chalk stacks formed by erosion.

questions.question: What does differential erosion mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Differential erosion means rocks erode at different rates because some are more resistant than others.

Sediment is added to a beach

questions.question: Explain why a cliff collapses during wave-cut platform formation.
questions.modelAnswer: The notch at the cliff base deepens until the cliff above is unsupported, so it collapses under its own weight.

questions.question: Put these landforms in order: stack, cave, stump, arch.
questions.modelAnswer: The correct order is cave, arch, stack, stump.

questions.question: Why is Old Harry Rocks a useful example for this topic?
questions.modelAnswer: It is a named UK example of chalk stacks formed as waves eroded weaknesses in a headland through the cave, arch, stack and stump sequence.

data.sourcePassage: Coastal hazards include flooding and erosion. Flooding happens when seawater covers land that is usually dry. It can be made worse by storm surges, high tides, sea-level rise, low-lying land and destructive waves. Sea-level rise is linked to warmer water expanding and melting land ice adding water to the oceans. Erosion risk is higher where rocks are soft, beaches are narrow, waves are powerful, or human actions interrupt sediment supply. The Holderness Coast in East Yorkshire is one of the fastest-eroding coastlines in Europe. Much of it is made from soft boulder clay, which is easily eroded by North Sea waves. At Mappleton, rock groynes and rock armour protect the village and the B1242 road, but they may reduce sediment moving south.

questions.modelAnswer: Coastal flooding is when seawater covers land that is usually dry.

questions.modelAnswer: The Holderness Coast is in East Yorkshire, UK.

questions.question: Give two reasons why the Holderness Coast erodes quickly.
questions.modelAnswer: It has soft boulder clay cliffs and is attacked by powerful North Sea waves, especially during storms.

questions.question: How can sea-level rise increase coastal risk?
questions.modelAnswer: Higher average sea level can make high tides, storm surges and coastal erosion more dangerous over time.

questions.question: Why might protecting Mappleton create conflict further south?
questions.modelAnswer: Groynes trap sediment at Mappleton, so less sediment may move south by longshore drift, leaving downdrift beaches narrower and more exposed to erosion.

data.sourcePassage: Coastal management involves choosing how to respond to erosion and flooding. Hard engineering uses built structures such as sea walls, groynes, rock armour and gabions. These can provide strong local protection but may be expensive, look artificial or transfer erosion. Soft engineering works more with natural processes. Beach nourishment adds sand or shingle to widen a beach, dune regeneration helps dunes recover, and managed retreat allows selected land to flood or erode in a planned way. Sustainable coastal management should reduce risk, be affordable over time, protect habitats, consider future sea-level rise and involve local communities. Fieldwork helps geographers judge management by collecting evidence such as beach profiles, sediment size, longshore drift observations and environmental quality scores.
